title: Measures and Indicators of Health Status

questions.stem: In a town of 200,000, 40 people are diagnosed with disease X during a year, and 10 of them die of it. What is the case-fatality rate?
questions.explanation: CFR = deaths from the disease / diagnosed cases = 10 / 40 = 25%. A: 10/200,000 is the mortality rate. B: 40/200,000 is the proportion of the town with the disease. C: 30/40 is the proportion who survived. E: CFR is a proportion of diagnosed cases; no person-time is needed.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 8–9

questions.stem: Early in an outbreak only severe hospitalized cases are tested. Testing then expands to the community and finds many mild cases; the number of deaths is unchanged. What happens to the case-fatality rate (CFR) and the mortality rate?
questions.explanation: CFR = deaths / confirmed cases: the denominator grows while deaths stay constant, so CFR falls. Mortality rate = deaths / whole population: neither part changes. B: CFR changes because its denominator changes; the mortality rate doesn't. C: The mortality rate's denominator is the whole population, not confirmed cases. D: More confirmed cases lowers CFR. E: CFR's denominator has changed.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 10, 34

questions.stem: City 1 has a crude mortality rate of 296 per 100,000 and City 2 of 469 per 100,000. City 2's population is much older. What is the best conclusion?
questions.explanation: Crude rates are influenced by age structure; standardization removes this so populations can be compared fairly. A: The higher crude rate may simply reflect an older population. C: Only true after adjustment for age. D: CFR measures disease severity, not population mortality. E: Proportionate mortality is the fraction of deaths by cause and isn't a measure of risk.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 16–18, 35

questions.stem: A ministry wants to rank conditions by the total healthy life they cost the population, including low back pain, which rarely kills. Which measure fits best?
questions.explanation: DALYs = YLL + YLD, combining premature death and disability; low back pain's burden is almost all YLD. A: QALYs measure health gained by an intervention. B: Life expectancy summarizes a whole population, not the burden of one condition. D: Counts deaths only. E: Counts deaths only.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 28–30

questions.stem: Without treatment, a patient will live 4 years at a utility weight of 0.5. With a new treatment, the patient will live 6 years at a utility weight of 0.75. How many QALYs does the treatment gain?
questions.explanation: QALY = years × utility: without = 4 × 0.5 = 2; with = 6 × 0.75 = 4.5; gain = 2.5 QALYs. A: QALYs without treatment (also the extra life-years alone). B: QALYs with treatment. C: The change in utility weight alone. D: Applies the utility gain to the original 4 years only and ignores the 2 extra years.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 31–32

questions.stem: Which measure of mortality uses total births (live births plus stillbirths) as its denominator?
questions.explanation: Perinatal and stillbirth rates use total births because the numerator includes stillbirths. A, C, D, E: These use live births.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slide 14

questions.stem: A region records 2,000 live births and 20 stillbirths in one year. Twelve infants die before 28 days and 8 die between 28 days and 1 year. What is the infant mortality rate?
questions.explanation: Infant mortality = deaths < 1 year / live births × 1,000 = (12 + 8) / 2,000 × 1,000 = 10 (= neonatal + post-neonatal). A: 12/2,000 is the neonatal rate. B: 8/2,000 is the post-neonatal rate. D: Uses total births; the infant rate uses live births. E: Adds stillbirths and uses total births.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 13–14

questions.stem: A small village wants to compare its mortality with the national population, but its age-specific death rates are unstable because each age group has very few deaths. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Direct standardization to a standard population

questions.explanation: Indirect standardization applies standard (national) rates to the study population; it is used when population-specific rates are unavailable or unstable and gives a standardized mortality ratio. A: Direct standardization needs reliable age-specific rates in each population. B: Crude rates ignore age structure. C: CFR measures disease severity. E: Proportionate mortality isn't a measure of risk.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 16, 18
